cases.notes: The second run of migrate_api_tables_begin is a no-op because table_exists(api_collections) && !has_column(api_collections, workspace_id) is now false (the column exists) — no re-rename, no duplicate copy. Every later step-migration function (add_*_to_*) is independently idempotent via its own has_column guard. A fresh database needs no legacy-rename path at all: migrate_api_tables_begin's needs_migration check is false because api_collections does not exist yet, so the schema batch alone creates it in its current (already workspace_id) shape.

steps: run the full migration procedure (migrations::run) against the seeded database (no workspaces row exists)
assert the legacy table and its one row are still present
run the full migration procedure again
assert the row is now migrated and the legacy table is gone
cases.notes: migrate_api_tables_finish returns early, leaving the *_legacy tables untouched, when no workspace row exists to assign the rows to — deleting a user's collections to tidy up a migration is treated as worse than leaving a legacy table behind. On the first run, migrate_api_tables_begin renames api_collections (and the other three roots) to *_legacy and the schema batch recreates empty replacements that already have workspace_id; migrate_api_tables_finish then finds no workspace and stops, so the *_legacy tables and their rows survive untouched between runs. On the second run (after a workspace now exists), migrate_api_tables_begin is itself a no-op — the live api_collections already has workspace_id, so its needs_migration guard is false and nothing is re-renamed — while migrate_api_tables_finish now finds a workspace, copies every *_legacy row across with that workspace's id, and drops the four *_legacy tables. It is migrate_api_tables_finish, not migrate_api_tables_begin, whose behaviour changes between the two runs.
